quiz.title: Chapter 3 Quiz: The Question Method
quiz.intro: Twelve questions on the cycle, the question types, the three tools, and closure. This is the chapter the rest of the book runs on.

items.q: The five steps of the cycle, in order, are:
options: Search, read, cite, write, repeat
Write your research question; research to answer it; write down what you found; identify your next question; repeat
Identify the issue; find a secondary source; find a case; find a statute; write
Clarify, review, reflect, prepare, search
items.why: Five steps and intermittent checkpoints: the steps keep you moving, the checkpoints keep you thinking (The Five Steps and Intermittent Checkpoints).

items.q: The legal issue, the macro question, and a research question differ how?
options: They are three names for the same thing
The legal issue is the problem; the macro question is that issue framed as the one big question your document answers; a research question is a micro question you answer along the way
The macro question is always a statute; research questions are always cases
Research questions are written only at the planning stage
items.why: When this book says research question it always means the micro question; the macro question is the destination and research questions are the steps (Introduction; The Role of Questions).

items.q: “What is the federal definition of ‘organic’?” is which type of question?
options: Exploratory (no-clue)
Definitional
Application (fact-finding)
Focusing
items.why: It asks what a term means. The statute hands definitional authority to the USDA, so the next question becomes what the USDA’s definition is (Definitional Questions).

options: I have a contract dispute; where do I even start?
What are the elements of promissory estoppel?
What is the standard for reasonable accommodation under the ADA?
Have courts found a school newspaper to be a public forum on facts like mine?
items.why: Focusing questions ask for the specific rule, standard, or test and usually cross from secondary to primary authority. (The first is no-clue exploratory, the second foundational exploratory, the last application.)

items.q: The three kinds of exploratory question are:
options: Definitional, focusing, and application
No-clue, foundational, and survey
Fact-finding, constructive, and survey
Primary, secondary, and tertiary
items.why: No-clue questions come first in an unfamiliar area; foundational questions seek the structure of the law; survey questions ask how multiple jurisdictions handled an issue (Exploratory Questions).

items.q: The Research Log has seven fields. Which list is correct?
options: Research Question, Question Type, Method, Findings, Source Consulted, Next Question, Notes
Issue, Rule, Explanation, Application, Conclusion, Citation, Notes
Question, Search String, Results, Answer, Next Steps, Date, Notes
Macro Question, Micro Question, Source, Holding, Dictum, Next Question, Notes
items.why: Seven fields, and the macro question written once at the top (The Research Log).

items.q: Of the three tools, which holds the questions still to be answered?
options: The research log
The annotated outline
The research map
The search log
items.why: The map tells you where you are going, the log where you have been, and the outline what you know. The map holds questions; the outline holds answers (Three Tools, One Process).

items.q: “Is our newspaper school-sponsored?” is, according to the chapter:
options: A research question you should run next
Not a research question at all: no database can answer it, so it is a writing step captured in a bracketed note on the outline
A definitional question
A survey question
items.why: An application question in research asks how courts applied a rule to facts; applying the rule to your own facts is writing, done during a research pause (A Research Pause).

items.q: A paragraph in a finished opinion supports one point of law with a string of citations. That usually signals:
options: A settled point nobody is fighting about
A survey question answered by looking across many cases
A definitional question
An error by the court
items.why: Settled points usually rest on a single citation; a string of citations usually means a survey across scenarios (Reverse Engineering the Question).

options: You have run out of time
You have run out of new sources
The research is substantively complete: the governing rule is identified, applied to your facts, counterarguments addressed, and more research would change only your wording
Your supervisor told you to stop
items.why: Running out of sources is not closure. Practical closure, by contrast, is an external constraint forcing a stop, which you document (When Is Your Research Done?).

items.q: The Nix v. Hedden tomato case is used to show:
options: That tomatoes are legally fruit
How the question types trade places: a definitional question comes back empty, a focusing question supplies the reading rule, and an application question closes it
That dictionaries control statutory meaning
That tariff law is common law
items.why: The Tariff Act defined neither word, the Court held ordinary meaning governs, and then asked whether a tomato is a vegetable in common speech (The Types in Motion).

items.q: “What is the Tinker standard, and does it apply to school publications?” should be:
options: Run as written; it is one question
Split into two questions, each with its own answer, source, and log entry
Skipped because Tinker is old
Answered from a dictionary
items.why: One question per question mark. A compound question is two cycles (Q1: Explore the Legal Landscape).
